sections.h2: What happens when property tax goes unpaid in North Carolina?
sections.html:
The taxing unit holds a lien on the parcel, and it can advertise the lien and then force a sale through the courts. Chapter 105 of the General Statutes sets out each step, and the owner can stop the process by paying until the sale is confirmed or, in one route, until execution issues.

North Carolina counties and cities handle the sale themselves. The tax collector for the county or the town advertises the lien, a court proceeding follows, and a commissioner or the sheriff sells the property at public auction. An owner who wants any say in the price has to act before that sale is scheduled.

The lien itself exists from the date the property was to be listed for tax. G.S. 105-355 adds penalties, interest and costs to it at the same moment. A bill that is due September 1 is paid at face value through the following January 5, and G.S. 105-360 then adds 2 percent through the end of January and three-fourths of one percent for each month or fraction after that.

sections.h2: How and when does the tax collector advertise the lien?
sections.html:
Advertising runs between March 1 and June 30, after the collector reports unpaid real property taxes to the governing body in early February. G.S. 105-369 sets that calendar: a county collector reports on the first Monday in February, a municipal collector on the second Monday.

Before the ad runs, the collector mails a notice to the record owner at the last known address by first-class mail, at least 30 days ahead of publication. The notice states the unpaid principal and warns that the owner's name will appear in a newspaper ad. The statute also says a mistake in mailing that notice does not void the lien or a later foreclosure, so an owner who moved should keep the tax office updated.

  • The county posts the notice at the courthouse and publishes each lien at least once in a newspaper of general circulation. A city posts at city or town hall.
  • The ad lists the record owner as of the delinquency date, a short parcel description and the principal amount, and says interest and costs will be added.
  • Each advertised parcel carries an advertising fee that counts as tax.
  • A parcel comes off the list when the owner pays the tax, accrued interest and a share of the advertising fee during the advertising period.

sections.h2: What are the two foreclosure routes?
sections.html:
A taxing unit can sue to foreclose under G.S. 105-374, or it can docket a certificate of taxes as a judgment under G.S. 105-375. Which route applies depends on the choice the governing body made, so ask the collector for your parcel.

The 105-374 route is a court action filed in the county where the land lies, in the nature of a mortgage foreclosure. The owner of record, the spouse and other lienholders are served. The 105-375 route is the in rem alternative, which the statute describes as a simple and inexpensive way to enforce taxes. The table below sets the two side by side using the statute text.

How G.S. 105-374 and G.S. 105-375 differ on the points that affect an owner
PointG.S. 105-374 actionG.S. 105-375 judgment
StartForeclosure action filed where the land liesCertificate of taxes filed with the clerk of superior court no earlier than 30 days after the liens were advertised
Notice to ownerService on owner, spouse and lienholdersCertified or registered mail at least 30 days before docketing, with follow-up posting or newspaper notice if no receipt returns in 10 days
Added costsCommissioner fee up to 5 percent of the purchase priceMailing and publication costs plus a $250 administrative charge
SalePublic auction at the courthouse doorSheriff sale on execution, issued after three months and before two years from indexing
Last day to payBefore the court confirms the saleBefore execution issues, by paying or moving to set aside

Sources for the table: G.S. 105-374 and G.S. 105-375.

sections.h2: What happens at the sale itself?
sections.html:
The property goes to the highest bidder at public auction, and the buyer receives fee simple title free of most liens. Under 105-374 the commissioner can require a deposit of up to 20 percent of the bid and must report the sale within three days. Anyone may file exceptions or an increased bid within 10 days after the report, and confirmation can be requested once those 10 days run.

Under 105-375 the sheriff sells as in any execution sale, with two differences. The owner has no debtor's exemption, and the sheriff mails notice at least 30 days before the sale to the taxpayer and every lienholder of record. The buyer takes the property free of claims except other unpaid taxes or special assessments, C-PACE assessments and conservation agreements.

The statute for the 105-375 route also adds a clerk's fee out of the sale proceeds. Attorney fees for the taxing unit are arranged separately and the statute says they cannot be added to the judgment as costs.

sections.h2: Can an owner redeem the property or stop the sale?
sections.html:
Yes. In a 105-374 action, a person redeeming before confirmation pays all taxes due on the parcel plus penalties, interest and costs, and any sale money left after the taxes goes to the court for the people entitled to it. In a 105-375 case, the owner or anyone with an interest can ask the clerk to set the judgment aside before execution issues if the tax was paid or the lien is invalid, and paying the judgment in full ends it.

  • Pay before the advertisement: the parcel never appears on the list.
  • Pay after the ad runs: add the accrued interest and a share of the advertising fee.
  • Pay after a judgment is docketed: add interest at 8 percent plus the costs and the $250 charge.
  • Pay before confirmation in a 105-374 sale: add penalties, interest and all costs.

Because the amounts change at each stage, ask the tax collector for a written payoff figure with an end date. That number is also what a title company will want if you sell.

sections.h2: What if the county or city buys the property?
sections.html:
A taxing unit may bid at the sale, and if it wins it can resell the parcel later. G.S. 105-376 lets the unit pay only the part of its bid that would not go back to the taxing units as tax, penalties, interest and costs. It then holds the property for every unit with an interest and uses net income and resale money first to repay its own outlay.

The same statute allows a resale by private sale to the former owner or another person who had an interest, for an amount not less than the unit's interest, if the governing body approves. Ask the tax office whether it takes that kind of offer before assuming the sale ended your rights.

sections.h2: Why sell the house before a tax foreclosure sale?
sections.html:
A private sale lets you set the timing and keep any value above the debt. At auction the price is whatever the room bids, and the costs listed above come out of it first.

  • Get a payoff statement for every taxing unit, since a county and a town may each hold a lien on the same parcel.
  • Record the deed promptly. G.S. 47-18 says a conveyance is not valid against lien creditors or purchasers for value until it is registered in the county where the land lies.
  • Budget for the deed excise tax. G.S. 105-228.30 sets it at one dollar for each $500 of value or fraction of $500, paid by the seller to the register of deeds before recording.
  • Expect the recording fees in G.S. 161-10: $26 for the first 15 pages of a deed and $4 for each added page.

If the house needs work, has tenants, or came through an estate, a buyer who closes with cash and takes the property as is can simplify the payoff. Ask the closing agent to pay the tax payoff out of the proceeds, and the register of deeds then records the new deed.

faqs.q: Does North Carolina sell tax liens to investors?
faqs.a: The statutes describe foreclosure and sale of the property itself, with the taxing unit as lienholder and the buyer taking title at the sale. G.S. 105-369 through 105-376 do not set out a certificate sale to private investors, so ask your county tax collector how it collects delinquent real estate tax.

faqs.q: When are unpaid property taxes advertised?
faqs.a: Advertising takes place between March 1 and June 30. The collector reports unpaid real property tax to the governing body in February, mails the owner a notice at least 30 days before publication, and then posts and publishes the list.

faqs.q: Can I still pay after the lien is advertised?
faqs.a: Yes. During the advertising period a parcel comes off the list when the owner pays the tax, accrued interest and a share of the advertising fee. After a foreclosure starts, payment of taxes, penalties, interest and costs still ends it before confirmation under 105-374, or before execution under 105-375.

faqs.q: Does the buyer at a tax sale get a clean title?
faqs.a: Mostly, yes. The buyer takes fee simple title free of most claims and liens. Other unpaid taxes or special assessments, C-PACE assessments and conservation agreements can survive, so a buyer should ask a title company about them.

faqs.q: What does the 105-375 judgment cost an owner on top of the tax?
faqs.a: The judgment adds interest at 8 percent a year, the mailing and publication costs and a $250 administrative charge. A tax collector can give the exact total for your parcel on a given date.
